strengths: Addresses an important asymmetry in vision-language alignment: hierarchical text features are aligned with only a single visual feature, which is suboptimal for taxonomic tasks.
The semantic-aware visual feature extraction framework using intermediate ViT class tokens and text-guided cross-attention is intuitive, and ablations show consistent improvements over ProTeCt.
Extends hierarchical alignment to hyperbolic manifolds with modality-specific curvatures and an intermediate manifold, which is a promising research direction.
Experiments are broad: four datasets, few-shot and base-to-novel/base-to-whole settings, three metrics, and multiple prompt-learning and hyperbolic baselines.
Reproducibility efforts are substantial, including dataset preprocessing, training details, hyperparameters, proofs, and a commitment to release code and models.
Visualizations (t-SNE and GradCAM) provide qualitative evidence that the method learns more separable and semantically meaningful hierarchical features.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation of the heterogeneous manifold distance is questionable: KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions on different manifolds is not well-defined in the standard sense, and the derived distance in Eq.(9) relies on an ad hoc Taylor expansion and a numerical constant y1*. The existence/uniqueness proofs also require unverified large-r conditions, so the central theoretical claim is not rigorously established for practical settings.

Ablation results indicate that most of the performance gain comes from the semantic-aware visual feature extraction (Ours-Euc), while the proposed heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment provides only small or inconsistent additional improvements, undermining the paper's main claimed contribution.

The distinction between the full method and the Ours-HypV2 variant is unclear, making it difficult to assess what exactly the intermediate manifold search contributes beyond independently learnable curvatures.

Evaluation lacks statistical significance: results are averaged over three runs but no standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported, and there is no sensitivity analysis for curvature initialization, intermediate-layer choice, or the entailment loss weight alpha.

Baseline adaptation for hyperbolic methods such as MERU and HyCoCLIP is insufficiently described, and the very large performance gaps raise concerns about whether comparisons are fair for taxonomic open-set classification with hierarchical prompts.

The manuscript contains several clarity and correctness issues, including an incorrect update for c2 in Eq.(18), wrong curvatures in Algorithm 2's feature mapping, and typographical errors such as 'villina' and 'Trecut', which reduce confidence in reproducibility.

Claims are stronger than the evidence: the paper states it proves existence and uniqueness of the optimal intermediate manifold, but the proof relies on strong unverified assumptions; similarly, 'consistently outperforms' obscures the marginal gains from the hyperbolic component.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing ideas such as intermediate-layer token usage, cross-attention, hyperbolic entailment, and prompt tuning, with the main new algorithmic piece delivering limited empirical benefit.

strengths: Proposes a novel framework to construct hierarchical visual features from intermediate ViT layers using text-guided cross-attention, addressing the asymmetry between single visual features and hierarchical textual features in existing VLMs.
Extends hyperbolic alignment to heterogeneous manifolds with distinct learnable curvatures and introduces an intermediate manifold optimization, which is an interesting and underexplored direction.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation on four datasets (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), multiple few-shot and base-to-novel/whole settings, and three hierarchical metrics, with consistent improvements over strong baselines like ProTeCt.
Includes ablation studies, qualitative visualizations, and a reproducibility statement with implementation details and dataset preprocessing.
The idea of aligning tree-like features across modalities is well-motivated and could inspire future work on hierarchical vision-language alignment.
weaknesses: Theoretical foundation is weak: KL divergence between distributions on different hyperbolic manifolds is ill-defined because the sample spaces differ; the derivation uses questionable Taylor approximations, an ad hoc expansion point chosen to force the minimum, and assumes E_P[x]=u1, which is not generally true for wrapped normal distributions.

The existence and uniqueness proofs rely on unverified assumptions (e.g., sufficiently large r) and do not guarantee practical validity. The paper overclaims rigorous theoretical guarantees for the optimal intermediate manifold.

The core contribution of heterogeneous manifold alignment is not convincingly supported by the experiments: ablation shows Ours-HypV1 (single curvature) and Ours-HypV2 (heterogeneous) often perform similarly, with only marginal gains over Ours-Euc; most improvement comes from the semantic-aware feature extraction, not the hyperbolic alignment.

Evaluation is limited to taxonomic open-set classification; no direct measurement of modality alignment (e.g., retrieval, zero-shot transfer) is provided. The comparison to hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) may be unfair as they are not adapted to the TOS or prompt-learning setting.

Many technical errors and typos reduce clarity and reproducibility: Eq. (18) updates c2 using dJ/dc1 instead of dJ/dc2; Algorithm 2 has incorrect curvature indices; Eq. (13) uses t_i^{c2} instead of c3; tables contain 'villina' instead of 'vanilla'; inconsistent notation for base points in exponential maps.

The semantic-aware visual feature extraction framework lacks detailed ablation: no study on the number/choice of intermediate layers, cross-attention design, or the mapping strategy. The gains could be due to additional parameters/training rather than the proposed mechanism.

Potential overfitting: on Rare Species, base-class gains are large but novel-class gains are small, suggesting limited generalization. Abstract claims of up to 28.83% HCA improvement are not clearly tied to a specific baseline/setting and appear inconsistent with the tables.

Curvature optimization lacks constraints (e.g., positivity) and numerical stability discussion; golden section search combined with implicit gradients may be sensitive and computationally costly, with no convergence analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important problem: the asymmetry between hierarchical textual features and single visual features in vision-language models. The proposed semantic-aware visual feature extraction framework using intermediate ViT layers and text-guided cross-attention is a novel and reasonable approach.

The heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment idea, with distinct learnable curvatures for text and visual trees and an intermediate manifold, is conceptually interesting. The derivation of a KL-based manifold distance and the use of implicit differentiation for curvature optimization are technically sophisticated.

Experiments are extensive: four datasets (CIFAR-100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species), few-shot settings (1-shot, 16-shot), and base-to-novel/base-to-whole generalization, with three hierarchical metrics (LA, HCA, MTA). The method consistently outperforms strong baselines such as ProTeCt, MaPLe, and PromptSRC, with particularly large gains on HCA.

Ablation studies and visualizations are provided to analyze the contribution of the semantic-aware visual feature extraction and hyperbolic constraints. The visualizations of attention maps across taxonomic levels are insightful.
Reproducibility efforts are commendable: detailed appendix with proofs, training algorithms, hyperparameters, data preprocessing, and base/novel tree construction procedures.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation of the heterogeneous manifold alignment is questionable. The derived manifold distance D_L in Eq. (9) can become negative and is unbounded below as c3 -> 0, contradicting its stated interpretation as an affine transformation of a nonnegative KL divergence. Proposition 1 claims the minimum is uniquely at c3 = c1, but this is false without restricting c3 >= c1. The optimization in Eq. (7) lacks explicit constraints, yet the existence/uniqueness proofs rely on unstated bounds and Taylor approximations, undermining the central theoretical claim.

The hyperbolic/heterogeneous manifold component appears to yield only marginal empirical improvements over simpler hyperbolic variants (Ours-HypV1, Ours-HypV2) and even the Euclidean variant. In the ablations, differences are often within 0.1–1%, suggesting that most gains come from the visual feature extraction rather than the proposed heterogeneous manifold alignment. This weakens the paper's main claim and the significance of the core algorithmic contribution.

Several technical details are unclear or contain errors. Eq. (18) incorrectly updates c2 using c1 and dJ/dc1 instead of dJ/dc2. Eq. (15) and (16) have inconsistent curvature indices for textual features (using c2 instead of c1). Eq. (13) references c2 in the exterior angle formula. The selection of intermediate layers (4th and 7th) is not ablated, and the construction of hierarchical textual features from prompts is not fully specified.

The comparison with hyperbolic baselines MERU and HyCoCLIP may not be entirely fair, as these methods are not designed for the same prompt-learning TOS protocol. No statistical significance tests are reported, and some base-to-novel improvements are small (e.g., ImageNet novel LA 75.88 vs 75.42).

The method introduces many hyperparameters (intermediate layers, initial curvatures, alpha, k, treecut sampling) but only limited sensitivity analysis is provided. The practical complexity may hinder adoption.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of existing vision-language alignment methods: asymmetric alignment where text has hierarchical features but images are represented by a single feature.

Proposes a semantic-aware visual feature extraction framework that uses intermediate ViT layers and text-guided cross-attention to produce coarse-to-fine visual features; ablations show this component contributes substantial gains over ProTeCt.
Introduces heterogeneous hyperbolic manifolds with learnable modality-specific curvatures and an intermediate manifold, an interesting direction for geometric multimodal alignment.

Conducts extensive experiments across four datasets, multiple settings (few-shot, base-to-base, base-to-novel, base-to-whole), three metrics, and numerous ablations, sensitivity, and efficiency analyses.
Reports consistent improvements over strong baselines (MaPLe, PromptSRC, ProTeCt) across most settings, with especially large gains on Rare Species.
Provides a reproducibility statement with detailed hyperparameters, preprocessing steps, proofs, and plans to release code/models.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation of the heterogeneous manifold alignment is questionable: the KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions on different hyperbolic manifolds is not well-defined without a common dominating measure or an explicit mapping between manifolds. The derivation assumes the Fréchet means correspond to the same tangent vector, which is not generally true, so the derived distance D_L depends only on curvatures under a strong special-case assumption.

The proofs of Theorem 1 and Proposition 2 rely on conditions on the constant r (e.g., r > certain thresholds) that are not shown to hold in practice; r is estimated per batch, and the paper does not report typical r values or verify the convexity/uniqueness conditions empirically.

The specific contribution of the intermediate manifold search is marginal: ablations show Ours-HypV2 (independent learnable curvatures without intermediate manifold) performs nearly identically to the full method on Cifar100 and SUN (e.g., HCA 69.33 vs 69.38; 68.65 vs 68.67), with meaningful gains only on Rare Species. This weakens the central claim about the heterogeneous manifold algorithm.

The semantic-aware feature extraction, while effective, is not highly novel: using intermediate Transformer layers for coarse-to-fine features is established, and the text-guided cross-attention is a reasonable but incremental extension. The overall pipeline combines existing prompt learning, hyperbolic entailment, and cross-attention.

Evaluation lacks controls for parameter count/capacity: the cross-attention module adds parameters, so gains over ProTeCt may partly reflect increased capacity. A parameter-matched baseline would strengthen the attribution of gains to the proposed hierarchical alignment.

Clarity and presentation issues in the main paper: several equations contain typos or malformed expressions (e.g., Eq. 1 uses subscript v instead of x; Eq. 13 has a misplaced brace), and the strong assumptions behind the theoretical results are not clearly stated in the main text.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: asymmetric modality alignment in hierarchical vision-language tasks such as taxonomic open-set classification.
Proposes a symmetric feature-tree construction for both image and text modalities, rather than aligning hierarchical text with a single visual feature.

The semantic-aware visual feature extraction framework using intermediate ViT layers and text-guided cross-attention is plausible, and the ablation suggests this component provides the largest empirical gains.

Integrates hyperbolic geometry with learnable modality-specific curvatures and an intermediate-manifold construction, which is an interesting direction for modeling heterogeneous hierarchical geometries.
Reports experiments on four datasets and multiple settings (few-shot, base-to-base/base-to-novel/base-to-whole), with ablations, visualizations, efficiency analysis, and several appendix studies.
Results show consistent improvements over ProTeCt-style prompt-tuning baselines, especially on hierarchical consistency metrics in some settings.
The appendix contains substantial additional material, including proofs, dataset preprocessing details, ablation studies, and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation is questionable. KL divergence between wrapped-normal distributions defined on different hyperbolic manifolds is not well-defined without a common dominating measure or explicit transport. The proof approximates this by evaluating distances for points on one manifold under another manifold's metric, which is not mathematically valid.

The derivation of D_L assumes E_P[x] = u1 (the Fréchet mean equals the ambient Euclidean expectation), which is generally false for wrapped normal distributions on hyperbolic space. It also assumes u1 and u3 share the same tangent-space vector, which is a very strong and unjustified simplification.

The resulting D_L is explicitly not a metric (asymmetric and violates triangle inequality), yet it is used to define an 'optimal intermediate manifold' and to prove existence/uniqueness. The propositions rely on restrictive conditions on r and curvature bounds that are not shown to hold in practice.

The empirical gains from the heterogeneous manifold alignment are small. Ablations show Ours-Euc already captures most of the improvement over ProTeCt, while the hyperbolic variants and intermediate-manifold search add only marginal gains, sometimes within noise. This undermines the paper's central claim about the importance of heterogeneous manifold alignment.

Conceptually, the method does not truly align features between the two learned modality-specific manifolds L^{c1} and L^{c2}. Instead, it re-embeds the original Euclidean features into an intermediate manifold L^{c3}. Thus c1 and c2 mainly affect in-modal constraints, not the cross-modal alignment, weakening the claimed 'heterogeneous manifold alignment'.

The experiments lack error bars or statistical significance tests despite reporting average over three runs. Many claimed improvements over ProTeCt are small, and some base-to-novel results are equal or only marginally better.

Baselines are limited mainly to MaPLe/PromptSRC + ProTeCt. Hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) appear only in the appendix and likely use different training protocols, making comparisons difficult. Recent hierarchical/open-vocabulary methods such as BioCLIP-style models are not adequately compared in the main tables.

Evaluation protocol raises concerns. The base-to-novel split and 10-epoch training schedule appear tuned to avoid novel-class degradation. Rare Species uses concatenated full taxonomic paths as labels, which may inflate textual discriminability and make the task easier than standard species-level TOS classification.

Clarity and reproducibility are weakened by typos and invalid equations, e.g., the exponential map equation, the exterior-angle formula, and Algorithm 2 with duplicated/incorrect update lines. Efficiency numbers such as '74 s per batch' are implausible or at least unexplained.

The paper is positioned as making strong theoretical contributions, but the theory is not central to the empirical success. The distance-measure ablation shows only minor differences between the proposed D_L and simple alternatives, further limiting the significance of the claimed manifold-distance formulation.

Broader impact on vision-language alignment is unclear: the method is evaluated only on taxonomic open-set classification, and its advantages on standard VLM alignment or open-world tasks remain unproven.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: existing VLM alignment is asymmetric because text is hierarchical while images are represented by a single feature.
Proposes a clear symmetric framework that constructs hierarchical visual features from intermediate ViT layers using text-guided cross-attention, and aligns textual and visual feature trees.

Introduces a novel heterogeneous hyperbolic manifold alignment idea with learnable modality-specific curvatures and an intermediate manifold, supported by theoretical statements and implicit differentiation for curvature gradients.

Extensive empirical evaluation on four datasets (Cifar100, SUN, ImageNet, Rare Species) under few-shot and base-to-novel/base-to-whole settings, using three hierarchical metrics (LA, HCA, MTA), with consistent improvements over strong baselines such as ProTeCt, MaPLe, and PromptSRC.

Good ablation studies isolating the semantic-aware feature extraction, hyperbolic constraints, and intermediate manifold search; additional analyses include sensitivity, efficiency, visualizations, and learned curvatures.
Reproducibility is well supported with detailed appendices covering datasets, training procedures, hyperparameters, proofs, and a commitment to release code/models.
Visualizations (t-SNE and GradCAM) provide qualitative evidence that the learned features capture hierarchical semantics and attend to taxonomically meaningful regions.
weaknesses: The theoretical foundation of the manifold distance is questionable: KL divergence between wrapped normal distributions defined on different hyperbolic manifolds is not well-defined without a common base measure, and the derivation uses a Taylor approximation plus an assumption that E_P[x]=u1, which is generally invalid for hyperbolic Fréchet means. This undermines the claimed soundness of Theorem 1.

Proposition 1 appears not to hold for small r; the formula for D_L can be negative and non-monotonic when r is small, so the claimed uniqueness/minimizer at c3=c1 only holds under strong, unverified conditions. Proposition 2 also relies on large-r assumptions that are not checked in experiments.

The practical benefit of the central intermediate manifold search is marginal: ablations show Ours-HypV2 (independent learnable curvatures) is often very close to Ours, and the hyperbolic component adds much less than the semantic-aware visual feature extraction. This weakens the significance of the paper's main hyperbolic contribution.

Comparison with hyperbolic baselines (MERU, HyCoCLIP) is relegated to the appendix and shows suspiciously large gaps, suggesting these baselines may be under-adapted or unfairly tuned for the TOS/prompt-learning setting. A competitive hyperbolic prompt-learning baseline is missing from the main tables.

There are inconsistencies and presentation issues: efficiency numbers in the main text (74s vs 74.5s, same memory) contradict the appendix (30% more time, 2% more memory); 74s per batch seems implausible; claims such as '28.83% improvement' are absolute percentage-point gains, not relative improvements; and some equations/algorithms contain typos or unclear notation.

Novelty is partly incremental: intermediate-layer features, cross-attention with text queries, and entailment cones are existing ideas. The main novel component (heterogeneous curvature alignment) is theoretically shaky and empirically only modestly beneficial over simpler curvature variants.

Evaluation is limited to taxonomic open-set classification; broader VLM tasks, cross-domain robustness, and real-world domain shift are not tested, despite being acknowledged as important limitations.

Main results lack error bars or statistical significance tests, and the method introduces multiple sensitive hyperparameters (intermediate layers, initial curvatures, alpha, r) whose robustness is only partially explored on Cifar100.
